title: Spectral Attention Steering for Prompt Highlighting
claim: Steering shifts embeddings in a consistent direction across many layers and heads, showing a shared latent direction exists.
layout: 3x3 grid of PCA scatter panels, each with arrows and a mean-shift arrow
description: A 3x3 grid of scatter plots. Each panel is titled with a layer and head, for example 'Layer 20 - Head 3 (Pairwise Shift)'. Axes are PCA Component 1 (x) and PCA Component 2 (y), with no tick labels. Each panel plots pairs of points, with green dots for positive and pink dots for negative representations. Thin grey arrows connect each pair to show the individual shift. One thick dark-blue arrow in each panel shows the mean displacement. A legend in the top right lists Positive, Negative and Mean shift. The scatter density and arrow lengths differ between panels. The mean arrow points in a coherent direction within each head, and its size varies. The eye goes first to the dark-blue arrow, then to the bundles of grey arrows.
caption: Visualisation of pairwise key embedding shifts across different (layer, head) in Qwen3-1.7B-Base via PCA. Positive vs. negative representations are plotted for 26 shared token spans. Grey arrows trace individual shifts; the dark blue arrow shows the average displacement.
abstract: Attention steering is an important technique for controlling model focus, enabling capabilities such as prompt highlighting, where the model prioritises user-specified text. However, existing attention steering methods require explicit storage of the full attention matrix, making them incompatible with memory-efficient implementations like FlashAttention. We introduce Spectral Editing Key Amplification (SEKA), a training-free steering method that tackles this by directly editing key embeddings before attention computation. SEKA uses spectral decomposition to steer key embeddings towards latent directions that amplify attention scores for certain tokens. We extend this to Adaptive SEKA (AdaSEKA), a query-adaptive variant that uses a training-free routing mechanism to dynamically combine multiple expert subspaces based on the prompt's semantic intent. Our experiments show both methods significantly outperform strong baselines on standard steering benchmarks while adding much lower latency and memory overhead, in compatibility with optimised attention.
